**Comprehension (Q. 76 - 80):** In the modern zeitgeist, the ascendancy of technology (1) ___ an aura of inexorability, fostering the notion that human agency is increasingly subordinate to algorithmic architectures. Proponents of technological determinism posit that innovation unfolds according to an autonomous trajectory, largely immune to ethical, cultural, or political intervention. This perspective, however, often (2) ___ the complexity of human intentionality, reducing societies to passive recipients of innovation rather than active co-creators. Conversely, advocates for humanistic autonomy assert that technology's deployment is invariably mediated through socio- political frameworks, reflecting collective choices rather than immutable laws of progress. The crux of the debate hinges upon whether innovation possesses an inherent teleology or whether it is a malleable construct subject to deliberate modulation. Indeed, to view technological development as (3) ineluctable is to diminish the scope of human volition. Moreover, the asymmetry of technological access across socio-economic strata complicates the deterministic narrative, suggesting that technologies evolve not merely through technical ingenuity but through contested arenas of power, privilege, and ideology. As artificial intelligence, genetic engineering, and quantum computing advance, the ethical imperative to assert governance and restraint (4) ___ ever more salient. In the absence of such stewardship, humanity risks enacting a form of (5) autopoiesis, wherein systems self-perpetuate without conscious human oversight or ethical anchoring. Thus, the resolution of this tension will critically influence not merely the architecture of future technologies but the very ontology of what it means to be human.
